To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the reduction of the sustained BLD signal in the auditory cortex with continuous sound reflects stimulus-dependent changes in blood oxygenation rather that blood volume-related effects.

the BOLD signal time course in human auditory cortex is characterized, by two components, and initial peak and a subsequent plateau, that the sustained BOLD response is reduced when the sound is presented in a continuous manner rather than in a pulsed manner, and that the reduction in the amplitude of the sustained plateau of the BOLD signal is accompanied by a reduction in the amplitude in the sustained plateau of blood volume levels.

(1) the BOLD signal in the auditory cortex can be divided into an initial transient peak, which is related to neuronal activity, and a subsequent sustained component, which is related primarily to the blood volume; and (2) the reduction in the BOLD signal during sustained stimulation is due to a decrease in blood oxygenation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new fMRI method that allows for a direct assessment of blood volume changes in auditory cortex in response to auditory stimuli.
the functional neuroanatomy of human auditory cortex and the underlying neurophysiological mechanisms of the fMRI BOLD signal in the auditory system.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the repetition rate of sound modulates the amplitude of the sustained fMRI response in the auditory cortex, and that the reduction of the sustained BLD signal is due to the decrease in blood oxygenation rather then the increase in blood volume.
the sustained BOLD response reflects a balance between oxygen consumption and oxygenation.

The main takeaway from our work is that

, when using repetition rate-modulated stimuli, one should be aware that the sustained BOLD response is modulated by the repetition rate of the stimulus and that this modulation can be attributed to changes in blood oxygenation.
, in addition to oxygenation, volume also contributes to the BOLD signal.
